text:
Here's the mental model, drawn from Anthropic's current caching docs.

## The problem it solves

The Messages API is **stateless**. There's no server-side session — every request resends the entire conversation: your system prompt, your tool definitions, and every prior turn. Turn 20 of a chat re-uploads turns 1–19.

Internally, the model has to do a forward pass over all those input tokens before it can generate the first output token (the "prefill"). That work is deterministic: the same input bytes always produce the same internal state. So it's cacheable — that's what prompt caching stores. On a hit, the server skips prefill for the cached span and charges you roughly a tenth of the input price for it.

Think of it as an HTTP cache where the key is the literal byte-prefix of your request body, not a URL.

## The one invariant

> **Caching is a prefix match. Any change anywhere in the prefix invalidates everything after it.**

The cache key is the exact bytes of the rendered prompt up to each breakpoint. One byte differing at position N invalidates every cache entry at position ≥ N. Not "mostly reuses" — invalidates. This is the same reason a Docker layer cache busts: layers are chained, so touching an early one rebuilds every layer below.

## Why order matters

The API renders your request in a fixed order:

```
tools  →  system  →  messages
```

That order is not negotiable, so it defines what "early in the prefix" means. Your job is to make **physical order match stability order**: things that never change go first, things that change every request go last.

The classic bug:

```python
system = f"You are a support agent. Current time: {datetime.now()}.\n\n{TEN_K_TOKEN_PLAYBOOK}"
```

That timestamp sits near byte 40. Every request produces a unique prefix, so the 10K-token playbook *and the entire conversation after it* are re-billed at full price, forever. You'll see no error — just a bigger invoice. The fix isn't a better cache marker; it's moving the timestamp to the end, into a message.

Same failure mode, less obvious:

- `json.dumps(schema)` without `sort_keys=True` — key order wobbles between processes, tools render at position 0, nothing ever caches.
- `tools=build_tools_for(user)` — a per-user tool list means a per-user prefix and no sharing across users.
- `if beta_flag: system += "..."` — each flag combination is a separate cache namespace.

There's a useful nuance: the API has **three cache tiers** (tools / system / messages) and a change only invalidates its own tier and below. So changing message content never touches the tools+system cache — but changing a tool definition rebuilds everything. Model switches also force a full rebuild, since caches are model-scoped.

## Breakpoints

Nothing is cached unless you ask. You mark a content block with `cache_control`, which means "cache everything from the start of the prompt up to here":

```python
system=[{
    "type": "text",
    "text": LARGE_STABLE_PROMPT,
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},   # caches tools + system together
}]
```

Rules worth knowing up front:

- **Max 4 breakpoints** per request.
- Place the breakpoint at the end of the **shared** portion, not the end of the whole prompt. If your prompt is `[big shared context][unique question]` and you mark the end, every request writes a distinct entry that's never read — you pay the write premium for nothing.
- There's a **minimum cacheable prefix**, model-dependent (512 tokens on Opus 5, up to 4096 on some others). Below it, caching silently no-ops.
- There's also a top-level `cache_control` on the request that auto-places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block — good default for growing conversations, wrong when the prompt ends in per-request content.

## TTL and pricing

Two TTLs: 5 minutes (default) and 1 hour (`"ttl": "1h"`). A read refreshes the timer for free, and the clock starts at the *beginning* of the request that touches it — so a 4-minute generation leaves only ~1 minute of headroom on a 5-minute entry.

| | Cost vs. base input |
|---|---|
| Cache write, 5-min TTL | 1.25× |
| Cache write, 1-hour TTL | 2× |
| Cache read | ~0.1× |

Break-even is 2 requests on the 5-minute TTL, 3 on the 1-hour. Pick by the **start-to-start gap** between requests sharing a prefix: under 5 minutes, stay on the default (each request refreshes it, so the 1-hour TTL buys you nothing but a doubled write); 5–60 minutes is the only window where 1-hour pays off.

## Verify it, and keep verifying it

Every response carries the ground truth:

```python
r.usage.cache_read_input_tokens      # served from cache (~0.1×)
r.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens  # written this request (1.25×/2×)
r.usage.input_tokens                 # full price — the uncached remainder only
```

Total prompt size is the **sum** of all three, which surprises people reading `input_tokens` alone.

The failure mode to design against is a silent regression: caching works when you build it, then six months later someone adds a dynamic field to the system prompt. Nothing breaks, no error fires, the bill just goes up. Worth an integration test asserting that a second identical request shows `cache_read_input_tokens > 0`.

One more thing you'll hit as a backend engineer: **concurrent requests don't share a warm cache**. An entry becomes readable only once the first response starts streaming, so N parallel requests with identical prefixes all pay full price. For fan-out, fire one request, wait for its first token, then release the rest.

If you want, I can walk through the caching layout for a specific service you're designing — the placement decisions get concrete fast once there's a real prompt-assembly path to look at.
